1:
Henry notices first that nobody called the meeting. No common head summoned them; they came by the consent of one common heart, fired with zeal for the honour of God and Israel. He thinks Mizpeh was chosen because Shiloh was small and the residence of the priests, so that the nation would not put so great an assembly upon it. Whether Mizpeh was itself a holy place is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch say the phrase unto the Lord proves no sanctuary there and no ark carried thither, only that the court was held in the sight of Jehovah. Clarke thinks the Lord was consulted there as well as at Shiloh, and cites the Maccabean record that in Maspha was the place where they prayed aforetime in Israel; yet he grants that before the Lord may mean no more than meeting in God's name. Ellicott sees no difficulty in the ark and Urim having been brought, since the chapter later carries them to Bethel, and identifies the site with the watch-tower the Crusaders called Mountjoie, from which a traveller first sees Jerusalem.

The reach of the summons and the size of the muster are both remarked on. Ellicott says from Dan to Beersheba, unless it is an anachronism of the writer, puts these events after the raid in which Dan took Laish; the tribes beyond Jordan came too, all but Jabesh-gilead. He gets an unexpected fact out of the four hundred thousand. At both wilderness censuses Israel numbered just over six hundred thousand; so the wars against the Canaanites had cost the nation a third of its strength, more than the wandering had, while Benjamin alone had grown. Henry reads the figure as a militia rather than a levy: all who drew sword, not hirelings nor pressed men, and only those spared from the land. Gill, Clarke and Ellicott all render the word for the chief men as corner-stones, and Clarke draws the two conclusions it invites, that the chiefs are the strength of the people as the corners are of the walls, and that Christ is therefore called the chief corner-stone.

Benjamin heard and did not come. Keil and Delitzsch infer their absence from the silence about their arrival, and from the later verse where the assembly must send men to call them to account. Ellicott supposes they had the same summons and insolently refused to notice it. Gill offers a range of motives: they may have wished to screen the offenders, or been careless and secure, imagining their brethren would never go to war over it, or too proud to answer. Henry regrets the lost opportunity, since a fair hearing might have prevented all the mischief that followed, but the notice hardened them instead. On the enquiry he is careful: a committee examined the witnesses, and though only the Levite's testimony is recorded, the plural in the original shows more than one was heard, as the law required, since no man might be put to death on a single witness.

The testimony itself is not taken at face value. Keil and Delitzsch point out that nobody at Gibeah had said they meant to kill the Levite; he draws that himself from what befell his wife. Ellicott says the same more bluntly, that circumstances have been left out and the Levite colours the whole story in the way most favourable to himself. Ellicott renders the offenders the lords of Gibeah, and suggests that if they were men in authority it explains both why nobody rescued the woman and why the town would not give them up. Gill observes that he takes the cutting up of the body upon himself, lest anyone suppose that outrage too had been theirs. Keil adds that the word for the crime is the law's term for lewdness punishable by death, and that the closing appeal means simply, make up your minds here and pass sentence.
8:
The vote is unanimous, and the commentators weigh its wording. Ellicott notes that the phrase rendered as one man is elsewhere translated with one consent, and suggests the oath about tent and house is worded for both kinds of Israelite, the tribes beyond Jordan being mostly graziers who lived under canvas. Clarke puts the sense of the oath bluntly: we will have satisfaction for this wickedness before we return home. On the next clause Ellicott doubts the received rendering. Our version follows the Greek in supplying we will go up by lot, which he compares to the sentence of the Amphictyonic council against the guilty city of Crissa; but he thinks it may rather mean casting the lot upon Gibeah, to divide its territory once taken. The provisioning is read the same way by all. A tenth of the muster, chosen probably by lot, was told off to carry victuals, which Clarke takes as a sign they expected a long contest, though Ellicott observes they anticipated no other difficulty than feeding themselves. Keil and Delitzsch note that the word added to as one man means as comrades and only strengthens it, and that the narrative here runs ahead of itself, what follows having come first in order of time.

The embassy to Benjamin comes next, and Henry thinks it the hinge of the whole tragedy. Had Benjamin come up to Mizpeh there would have been nobody to deal with but the men of Gibeah; by staying away they made the quarrel general. He is careful to say the Israelites were discreet in their zeal and did not suppose it would justify falling on a whole tribe, unless that tribe, by sheltering the criminals, made itself accessory after the fact. The demand itself was that Benjamin either punish the offenders or give them up, so that the evil might be put away and the infection stopped by cutting off the gangrened part; and Henry adds that since the sin was so like the sin of Sodom, they might justly fear the same hail from heaven if it went unpunished. He draws the rule that all methods of accommodation must be used before we go to war or go to law. Keil and Delitzsch say the same in legal terms, that the culprits were to be surrendered so the evil might be exterminated from Israel according to the law. Ellicott, Gill and Keil all note that the word for the tribes of Benjamin means its ten families.

Why Benjamin refused is the question. Clarke says nothing could have been fairer, since only the murderers were asked for, and takes the refusal to mean the tribe would have acted the same part had they been present, which proves them excessively depraved. Ellicott finds a likeness nearer home, in the spirit of solidarity that has often made a Highland clan defend a member guilty of some grave outrage; that they should prefer a civil war to giving up their criminals illustrates the peculiarly fierce character of the tribe, and their standing out against all Israel is like the courage in a bad cause of the Phocians in the sacred wars of Greece. Henry offers two explanations and does not choose between them. Either the tribe was more debauched than the rest, some of the most fruitful parts of Canaan having fallen to their lot, so that like Sodom in the garden of the Lord they became sinners exceedingly; or else, as Bishop Patrick suggested, they resented the interference and would not do their duty because reminded of it by brethren from whom they scorned to be taught. Either way, Henry says, they made the crime of Gibeah their own, and there is no cause so bad that it will not find some patrons. Keil and Delitzsch put it in a line: refusing a just demand, they took the side of the guilty.
14:
Both sides now muster, and the figures are disputed. Ellicott explains why Benjamin gathered out of the cities, since the Jebusites still held Jerusalem and the Canaanites round about were very incompletely subdued, so that town life was the only safe kind. He takes the twenty-six thousand for the true number, finding it in the Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic, while Clarke reports that Josephus and the Vulgate give twenty-five thousand and some Greek copies twenty-three. Ellicott draws the same melancholy conclusion here as he drew from the muster of the other tribes: Benjamin too had lost about a third of its strength since the last census, for all its exceptional increase in the wilderness. Keil and Delitzsch think neither number too large, since the whole congregation was in the field but for Jabesh-gilead, and the twelve tribes had counted above six hundred thousand fighting men in the days of Moses, so that not much more than two-thirds of them went out to this war.

The seven hundred slingers raise a harder question, since seven hundred men of Gibeah have just been counted too. Gill reports Ben Gersom's opinion that the two bodies are the same, and rejects it: the text puts the slingers among all this people, and it is not likely that every inhabitant of one town should be left-handed. Keil and Delitzsch reason the same way from the same words. Ellicott suspects the text itself, thinking it hard that one small city should furnish the whole choice contingent, and a curious coincidence that both figures should be exactly seven hundred; he notes that the phrase is missing from the Greek and the Vulgate altogether. Gill adds the irony that a tribe whose name means son of the right hand should have so many left-handed men, and that Josephus wrongly cuts the number to five hundred.

On the marksmanship the commentators are agreed and expansive. Clarke takes left-handed to mean ambidextrous, and stops at the phrase rendered not miss, which is literally not sin — the true import of the word, he says, since to sin is to miss the mark, and men miss the mark of happiness by aiming at sensual gratifications. He gathers the ancient reputation of the sling around the Balearic islanders, who would not let their children break their fast until they had struck the bread down from a pole, and who gave the sling its Greek name; he repeats the report of Ovid and Seneca that the leaden ball melted in the air from the friction of its own speed, and the statement of Vegetius that slingers could hit a mark at six hundred feet. Ellicott is drier. The phrase means only extreme accuracy of aim, and Bochart's attempt to explain it from archers shooting the horsehair crest off a helmet he calls learning fantastically misapplied. He adds that the sling is the natural weapon of a people poor and imperfectly armed, that Cyrus valued his four hundred slingers, and that the Balearic islanders once kept a Carthaginian fleet from anchoring with showers of stones. His last observation is tactical: a left-handed slinger strikes his enemy on the right, which is the undefended side.
18:
Where they went to enquire is disputed. Ellicott insists the phrase means Bethel and not the house of God, since the Hebrew for house of God is always another word, and the Greek and Syriac and Chaldee all read Bethel; he cannot say why the more central Shiloh was passed over. Keil and Delitzsch answer that question directly: Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood, lay too far from the seat of war, so the ark was brought to Bethel instead, on the northern border of Benjamin, a place already consecrated by God's appearances to Jacob. Clarke and Gill take the other view, that a deputation was sent to Shiloh, where Phinehas was. Ellicott sees no obstacle either way, since the high priest seems to have felt no scruple about carrying the ephod wherever it was wanted, as the ark itself was carried from place to place, and there is no need to suppose the tabernacle moved with them.

What they asked is as telling as where they asked it. Henry observes that they never enquired whether to go up at all, the case being plain, but only who should go first — which he takes to mean who should command, since the prince of the leading tribe would be general of the whole; had they meant the order of march they would have gone on to ask who should go next. He finds a reason for the answer, that the honour fell to Judah because our Lord was to spring from that tribe and in all things to have the pre-eminence, and a warning in it too, since the first post was the most dangerous and probably lost the most men: who would strive for precedency that sees the peril of it? Ellicott draws a different inference from the same answer. That the oracle could name a tribe shows the Urim and Thummim were something more than a pair of lots, and that the questions put to them were not only such as admit a yes or no. Clarke notices what the oracle did not say: the Lord said Judah, but he did not say that they should conquer.

The first battle goes against them. Ellicott explains how a small tribe held out, since the whole armed force of Benjamin had come in to save the town, and Gibeah stood on a hill, easily defended against the very imperfect siege operations of the ancients. Henry has the army caught between the Benjamites in front and the men of Gibeah sallying on their rear, and notes that no prisoners were taken because no quarter was given. Ellicott finds the slaughter of twenty-two thousand almost past belief, the defenders having nearly killed a man apiece. Henry will not let the defeat pass without accounting for it, and offers three answers together. God's judgments are a great deep and his way is in the sea, and we may be sure of the righteousness when we cannot see the reasons; the battle is not to the strong, and numbers are no arm to lean on; and God was correcting Israel for their own sins, for were there not with them, even with them, sins against the Lord their God? He adds a grim arithmetic, that the forty thousand the two defeats would cost was a tenth of the army, the same tenth they had drawn by lot to fetch victuals.
22:
Keil and Delitzsch describe the rally in words they borrow from an older commentary: the people strengthened themselves and drew up again in the very place where they had stood the first day, seeking out of pure vainglory to wipe out the stains and the disgrace their defeat had brought upon them. Gill sees a better motive in it as well, since their forces were still greatly superior and their cause was good, and Ellicott notes with the Vulgate that the confidence rested on their courage and their numbers. Before going out again they went up and wept before the Lord till evening. Keil and Delitzsch place the scene before the ark at Bethel and observe that the question had changed: the first time they asked which tribe should lead, and now they asked whether they should go up at all. Ellicott hears compunction in the way they name the enemy, Benjamin my brother, an uneasy sense that God might not approve a fratricidal war in spite of the first answer given by Urim. Both he and Keil are careful about the reckoning of days, since the second day means the second day of actual fighting, a day of supplication having fallen between the two engagements.

The second answer is as short as the first and the result is worse. Ellicott lays this defeat, like the one before it, to overweening confidence and carelessness, and works out what the two together had cost: forty thousand men of the eleven tribes, some thirteen thousand more than the whole Benjamite army numbered. Such a massacre he can only explain by supposing the slingers had some vantage-ground to shoot from, and he sets beside it the field of Crecy, where the French dead equalled the entire English force. Clarke states the reason more directly. It appears most evident that the Israelites did not seek the protection of God at all, but trusted in the goodness of their cause and in the multitude of their army, and God humbled them to teach that the race is not to the swift nor the battle to the strong. Gill finds the flaw in their mourning rather than their tactics, since they lamented the defeat and the loss of so many lives but not their own sins, and least of all the idolatry they had been guilty of. Keil and Delitzsch agree on where the fault did not lie: not in beginning the war, which the law they had themselves cited required of them, but in the spirit in which they went to it, as the repeated defeat was sent to show them.
26:
Henry names the two things Israel had leaned on and now lets go: the goodness of their cause and the superiority of their numbers. Both were real advantages, but they had depended on them so far as to neglect the duties they only now take up. Being sure their cause was good, they had thought it needless to ask God's blessing on it, perhaps concluding that he owed them his favour and could not in justice withhold it, since they had taken arms in defence of virtue. God has now shown them that he neither needed them nor was tied to them, and that they were more indebted to him for the honour of being ministers of his justice than he to them for the service. So they become petitioners at last. Before, they had only consulted the oracle; now they fast and pray and sacrifice. Clarke says the same by way of regret: had they humbled themselves and fasted and sacrificed at the first, they had never been discomfited. He notes that this is the earliest place in Scripture where fasting appears as a religious act, and adds that it is now little used, which he takes for a proof that self-denial is wearing out of fashion.

Ellicott fills in who was there and what was offered. All the people means the non-combatants too, and after two such battles the bereavement must have been almost universal. He distinguishes the sacrifices: the burnt offering was consumed entire and typified absolute self-dedication, while of the peace offering a part only was burnt and the rest might be eaten, its character being chiefly thanksgiving. Where they brought them is again the question of Bethel or Shiloh. Keil and Delitzsch take the remark about the ark to mean it was at Bethel only for a time, fetched from the tabernacle at Shiloh for this war; Gill reads the same verse as putting the scene at Shiloh. Ellicott holds that the ambiguity is created by the English rendering, which has hidden Bethel under the words house of God. He observes too that the earlier enquiry was made of Elohim and this one of Jehovah, and though he draws no certain inference from it, he thinks two terrible reverses had humbled the nation thoroughly and to its good.

The high priest's name fixes the date. Gill notes that Phinehas standing before the ark is the posture of the priest enquiring by Urim and Thummim, and that his presence proves the affair much earlier than the days of Samson, or the man must have been three hundred years old. Clarke identifies him with the Phinehas of Peor and dates the war shortly after Joshua's death. Ellicott makes more of the coincidence than either. That the grandson of Aaron and the grandson of Moses are the chief figures of these two wild stories is a strange illustration of the disorder of the times, since the one is discharging the supreme functions of the high priest while the other, sunk to a poor wandering Levite, never goes near his powerful cousin but serves a schismatic image for a paltry wage. Only now does the answer carry a promise, and Ellicott marks it as the first: they had to learn that even in a religious war they could not rely on their own strength, and he sets against it Napoleon's remark that Providence usually favours the strongest battalion. Henry watches what the promise did to them. Being sure of their strength before, they had thought stratagem beneath them and expected to conquer by a strong hand; now they lay an ambush as their fathers had at Ai, which he thinks likeliest to succeed just after a defeat has flushed the enemy and made a feigned flight credible. The assurance of victory, he says, did not make them remiss or presumptuous but set every head and hand at work.
29:
Assurance of victory did not make them careless. Gill notes that though promised success they still thought proper to use means, and though their numbers were great they fell back on art, as Israel had at Ai; Josephus says the ambush was set at night. Clarke puts it as a principle: they knew the promise could be expected only in the use of the proper means, and so employed all their military skill. Ellicott calls the stratagem exceedingly simple and primitive, and notes that it had already served against Ai and against Shechem. Gill reckons the third day from the second battle rather than the day after it, the journey to the sanctuary and the fasting having taken longer. Ellicott explains the feint. The Israelites drew back along two highways, one running to Bethel and the other to a second Gibeah called Gibeah in the field; and the phrase about smiting the people means smiting the wounded, the Benjamites rushing in to finish men the slings had brought down. Clarke gives two reasons for drawing them out of the town. The ambush behind it was to enter and fire the city as soon as it was empty, and the slingers inside the walls had an advantage they would lose in open country. Ellicott adds a third, that the branching roads divided the pursuers and let the ambush cut off their retreat.

Where the flight was stopped is a place with a name worth having. Keil and Delitzsch translate Baal-tamar as palm-place and report that a small village of that name still stood near Gibeah in the days of Eusebius. Ellicott presses the name further. It can only have come from some famous and therefore solitary tree, and there was exactly such a tree between Ramah and Bethel, the palm of Deborah; so he supposes the pretended rout ran as far as that landmark, where the men saw the smoke-signal and turned on their pursuers. Clarke sets out the whole disposition as three divisions, one at Baal-tamar, one in ambush behind the city, and one skirmishing in front of it. The place the ambush broke from is harder. Keil and Delitzsch take the rare word for a bare treeless tract and read the plains of Geba; Ellicott lists what others have made of it — a proper name in the Greek, caves in the Syriac, and a reading one letter distant giving the west of Gibeah — and admits the word occurs nowhere else.

The end comes quickly and is told twice over. Keil and Delitzsch describe ten thousand picked men striking the pursuers in the rear, so that the fighting grew severe while Benjamin still did not know ruin was upon them; Ellicott glosses the phrase from the Vulgate, that destruction threatened them on every side. Gill will not let the stratagem take the credit: for all the art and the numbers and the valour, the victory was the Lord's, since until that day Benjamin, though far fewer, had never lost. Clarke does the arithmetic and finds the tribe destroyed entire but for the six hundred who reached the rock Rimmon. Then the narrative doubles back, and the two Germans and the Englishman differ on why. Keil and Delitzsch defend the text against critics who called the summary spurious or took the verses after it for a rival account, holding that they have simply overlooked a habit of Hebrew historical writing, which gives the general result as early as it can and fills in the particulars afterwards. Ellicott accepts the same order but explains it differently, either by compilation from several sources, one of which he thinks was a poem, or by the sheer age of the writing, which belongs to a time before the periodic style of history was invented — the style, he says, that a Roman would have called inconditus, the style of the oldest annals.
37:
The signal was smoke, and Ellicott takes the words of the verse for the actual terms of the agreement, quoted as they were struck. He notes the literal sense of the phrase, to multiply to cause to ascend, and prefers the margin's column or beacon to flame; he also records a variant in some manuscripts and the Greek which would make the signal a sword, and rejects it, since the flash of a blade could never be seen at that distance, though it would have made a parallel to the shield that flashed treasonably from Athens to the Persians before Marathon. Gill adds from the Jewish commentators that a time was fixed as well as a sign, the men in ambush to break out when the defenders had been drawn far enough from the city. Clarke states the plainer point about the whole passage, that from this verse to the end of the chapter we are given in detail the operations already reported in general.

Gill describes what the men in ambush did with the empty town, making so large a fire that the pillar of flame and smoke could be seen a great way off. Ellicott would again read column rather than flame, and notes that what the Benjamites saw behind them is literally the whole of the city going up, a very powerful expression for a general conflagration. Keil and Delitzsch complete the turn: Benjamin looked back, saw the city ascending towards heaven in smoke, and was terrified as Israel wheeled about upon them. Gill says the Israelites turned at the trumpet, or at the sight of the fire, or at both. Ellicott, who is following the composition rather than the fight, marks these verses as a retelling with more graphic detail of what was said before, and would have the reader treat a good part of them as parenthetical.

The flight goes north-east, into the desert that climbs from Jericho towards the mountains of Bethel. Keil and Delitzsch fix the direction and note that the battle overtook them on the way. Ellicott names the tract the wilderness of Bethaven and explains why they ran that way, since the first thought of fugitives on that side of the country was always to reach one of the fords of Jordan. The clause about those who came out of the cities he finds obscure, and reports that the versions render it differently; if our own is right, the sense must be that Benjamites who fled to their own towns were pursued there and cut down.
43:
Gill has them surrounded on every side, the army posted in several places and the country people coming out against them, and cites Josephus for their being cooped up in a hollow of a valley with no way out. On the phrase that describes the trampling, Ellicott admits defeat: the Hebrew has no preposition where our version supplies one, the Greek and Luther make it a place-name, others render it in their rest, and the Vulgate turns it into a line of its own, that there was no repose for the dying. He calls the verse obscure and its description strong and poetic. The reckoning is then given in stages. Keil and Delitzsch count eighteen thousand fallen in the field, five thousand gleaned along the high-roads, and two thousand more overtaken at Gidom, a place whose situation nobody knows and which the Vulgate therefore leaves out. Both they and Ellicott dwell on the word gleaned, a metaphor from the vintage, as though the pursuit were the gathering of what the main battle had left standing.

The rock Rimmon takes its name from the pomegranate, and Ellicott, noting how common the name is where the tree is common, identifies it with a steep cone of white limestone still called Rimmon, visible from every side; he adds that the six hundred may have dwelt in the rock quite literally, since the hill has four large caverns. Keil and Delitzsch place it fifteen Roman miles north of Jerusalem, on the authority of the old gazetteer, and find it surviving in the village of Rummon. Clarke observes what those six hundred came to mean, since it was by them alone that the tribe was preserved from utter extermination. Gill and Ellicott both notice that the totals do not quite meet, the slain and the survivors together falling a thousand short of the tribe's muster; both conclude, with Ben Gersom and Abarbinel, that the thousand must have fallen in the two earlier battles, since it is not credible that victories so complete cost Benjamin nothing.

What follows the battle is harder to write about than the battle. Keil and Delitzsch state it flatly: the Israelites turned from pursuing armed men to those of Benjamin who were unarmed and defenceless, and cut down men and cattle without quarter, from the towns outward to everything that was found. Ellicott will not let the short words hide what they mean, and spells it out — the absolute extermination of a whole tribe, men, women and children, cities and cattle, six hundred fugitives excepted — and calls it almost inconceivably horrible that thousands of poor women and innocent children should be butchered in cold blood in a war between brother Israelites. He observes that the tribe was put under the ban as though it had been Canaanite, as mercilessly as Jericho or Ai, and allows that the feelings of the victors had been exasperated both by their own losses and by religious horror at the crime. Then he weighs the act on both sides. Its good side is its motive, an intense horror of moral pollution; its evil side is its ruthless savagery; and in both it answers to the character of the priest who had stood before the ark. Clarke will allow no good side at all. The crime of Gibeah was great, but there was no adequate cause for the relentless extermination of a whole tribe, and in this there was neither justice nor judgment; and he lays it where the book itself lays it, that there was no king in Israel, no effective government, and no man with authority to repress the disorderly workings of the mob.
